question: A consulting firm completes a project for a client on March 28, 2024 and sends an invoice for ₹10 lakh. The client pays the invoice on April 25, 2024. Under accrual accounting, when should the firm recognise the revenue?
before: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognised when it is EARNED — i.e., when the service is delivered or the goods are transferred, regardless of when cash arrives. The firm completed the project on March 28, so the revenue belongs in FY24, not FY25. The unpaid invoice creates a Receivable on the March 31 balance sheet. Option A is wrong because that is cash basis accounting, which listed companies do not use. Option C is wrong because revenue recognition is event-driven, not calendar-driven. Option D is wrong because Ind AS does not allow management discretion on timing of recognition for a completed service. This single concept is what separates accrual from cash accounting and why a company can be profitable on the P&L while running out of cash.
after:
Concept: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognised when the service is delivered or the right to payment is established, regardless of when cash is received. Recognition is event-driven, not cash-driven.

Why this is correct: The consulting firm completed the project and delivered the service on March 28, 2024. At that moment, the revenue was earned and the firm obtained the right to receive payment. Under Ind AS (Indian Accounting Standards), revenue must be recognised when performance obligations are satisfied. The unpaid invoice creates an Accounts Receivable asset on the March 31 balance sheet, and the ₹10 lakh revenue is recorded in the P&L for FY24.

Why the others are wrong: Option A confuses accrual accounting with cash basis accounting—cash receipt on April 25 is irrelevant to revenue recognition under accrual principles. Option C is incorrect because revenue recognition is event-driven (tied to service delivery), not calendar-driven (tied to fiscal year-end); March 28 falls within FY24, so revenue belongs in that period. Option D is wrong because Ind AS mandates recognition at service delivery and does not permit management discretion on the timing of revenue for completed performance obligations.

Intuition: Accrual accounting separates the timing of revenue recognition from the timing of cash collection. This is why companies can report operating profit while holding large receivables or, conversely, can receive advance cash without recognising revenue. For equity researchers, understanding this distinction is critical—a growing accounts receivable balance signals the firm has earned revenue but not yet collected it, which affects cash flow analysis and working capital management.
